back: Combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation, from macromolecules to biomes (term popularised by Edward Wilson).
Diversity at the genetic level within a species over its distributional range; e.g. Rauwolfia vomitoria reserpine variation, 50,000 rice strains.
Diversity at the species level in a region, e.g. Western Ghats have greater amphibian species diversity than Eastern Ghats.
Diversity at the ecosystem level; India exceeds a Scandinavian country because of its variety of biomes.
Slightly more than 1.5 million plant and animal species described so far.
Global species diversity is about 7 million (conservative, scientifically sound).
8.1% of global species diversity on only 2.4% of land area; ~45,000 plant + ~90,000 animal species.
More than 70% of animal species are insects — 7 out of every 10 animals.
Species diversity generally decreases from equator towards poles; tropics (23.5° N to 23.5° S) harbour the most.
More evolutionary time (undisturbed), less seasonal/predictable environment (niche specialisation), more solar energy (higher productivity).
log S = log C + Z log A (rectangular hyperbola); Z 0.1-0.2 for small regions, 0.6-1.2 for continents.
Plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass and higher productivity.
Paul Ehrlich's analogy: removing too many species (rivets) weakens the ecosystem (aeroplane); key species are critical.
Four major causes of biodiversity loss: habitat loss/fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasion, co-extinctions.
Conserving the whole ecosystem to protect biodiversity at all levels (save the entire forest to save the tiger).
Removing threatened species to off-site settings: zoos, botanical gardens, cryopreservation, in-vitro fertilisation, tissue culture, seed banks.
34 world-wide (originally 25); cover <2% land but harbour huge species richness; 3 (Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya) in India; strict protection could cut extinction by ~30%.
14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks, 448 wildlife sanctuaries and many sacred groves.
Forest tracts set aside and totally protected under cultural/religious traditions; last refuges for rare plants (e.g. Meghalaya).
Present extinction rates are 100 to 1,000 times faster than pre-human times; if trends continue ~half of species may be wiped out in 100 years.
